edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Ἀγγέλους γὰρ καλέσαι μὴ ἀναλαβόντας τὴν ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπους περὶ αὐτῶν ἐπιστήμην οὐκ εὔλογον. ἵνα δὲ καὶ καθ᾿ ὑπόθεσιν ἡ περὶ αὐτῶν ἐπιστήμη θαυμάσιός τις οὖσα καὶ ἀπόῤῥητος καταληφθῇ, αὕτη ἡ ἐπιστήμη, παραστήσασα τὴν φύσιν αὐτῶν καὶ ἐφ᾿ οἷς εἰσιν ἕκαστοι τεταγμένοι, οὐκ ἐάσει ἄλλῳ θαῤῥεῖν εὔχεσθαι ἢ τῷ πρὸς πάντα διαρκεῖ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ διὰ τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν υἱοῦ θεοῦ· ὅς ἐστι „λόγος“ καὶ σοφία καὶ ἀλήθεια καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα λέγουσι περὶ αὐτοῦ αἱ τῶν προφητῶν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τῶν ἀποστόλων τοῦ Ἰησοῦ γραφαί. ἀρκεῖ δὲ πρὸς τὸ ἵλεως ἡμῖν τοὺς ἁγίους ἀγγέλους εἶναι τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πάντα πράττειν αὐτοὺς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἡ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν διάθεσις ἡμῶν, ὅση δύναμις ἀνθρωπίνῃ φύσει, μιμουμένη τὴν ἐκείνων προαίρεσιν, μιμουμένων αὐτῶν τὸν θεόν· καὶ ἡ πρὸς τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ λόγον κατὰ τὸ ἐφικτὸν ἡμῖν διάληψις, οὐκ ἐναντιουμένη τῇ τρανοτέρᾳ περὶ αὐτοῦ διαλήψει τῶν ἁγίων ἀγγέλων ἀλλ᾿ ἐπ᾿ ἐκείνην ὁσημέραι τῇ τρανότητι καὶ διαρθρώσει σπεύδουσα. ὡς μὴ ἀναγνοὺς δὲ τὰς ἱερὰς ἡμῶν γραφὰς ὁ Κέλσος ἑαυτῷ ἀποκρίνεται ὡς ἀφ᾿ ἡμῶν ὅτι ἄλλο τι γένος παρὰ θεοῦ φαμεν τοὺς καταβαίνοντας ἐπ᾿ εὐεργεσίᾳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀγγέλους καί φησιν ὡς τὸ εἰκὸς λεχθῆναι ἂν αὐτοὺς ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν δαίμονας· οὐχ ὁρῶν ὅτι τὸ τῶν δαιμόνων ὄνομα οὐδὲ μέσον ἐστὶν ὡς τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ἐν οἷς τινὲς μὲν ἀστεῖοι τινὲς δὲ φαῦλοί εἰσιν, οὔτ᾿ ἀστεῖον, ὁποῖόν ἐστι τὸ τῶν θεῶν, τασσόμενον οὐκ ἐπὶ φαύλων, ἐπὶ δαιμονίων ἢ ἐπὶ ἀγαλμάτων ἢ ἐπὶ ζῴων. ἀλλ᾿ ὑπὸ τῶν τὰ θεοῦ ἐγνωκότων ἐπὶ τῶν ἀληθῶς θειοτέρων καὶ μακαρίων. ἀεὶ δ᾿ ἐπὶ τῶν φαύλων ἔξω τοῦ παχυτέρου σώματος δυνάμεων τάσσεται τὸ τῶν δαιμόνων ὄνομα, πλανώντων καὶ περισπώντων τοὺς ἀνθρώπους καὶ καθελκόντων ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τῶν ὑπερουρανίων ἐπὶ τὰ τῇδε πράγματα.
thought_title: Why angels are not called demons
pass_a_gloss: For to call upon/invoke (καλέω) angels without having taken up (ἀναλαμβάνω) the knowledge (ἐπιστήμη) about them that is beyond men (ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπους) is not reasonable (εὔλογος). And even if by hypothesis (καθ᾿ ὑπόθεσιν) the knowledge about them, being something wonderful (θαυμάσιος) and secret (ἀπόρρητος), should be grasped (καταλαμβάνω), this knowledge, having presented (παρίστημι) their nature (φύσις) and over what things each are appointed (τάσσω), will not allow one to dare (θαρρέω) to pray (εὔχομαι) to another than to the God over all, sufficient (διαρκής) for all things, through our Saviour (σωτήρ) the Son (υἱός) of God; who is 'Word' (λόγος) and wisdom (σοφία) and truth (ἀλήθεια) and as many other things as the writings of the prophets of God and of the apostles of Jesus say about him. And it suffices, for the holy angels of God to be gracious (ἵλεως) to us and for them to do everything on our behalf, our disposition (διάθεσις) toward God, as far as is possible (ὅση δύναμις) for human nature, imitating (μιμέομαι) their deliberate choice/purpose (προαίρεσις), they themselves imitating God; and our conception (διάληψις) concerning his Son the Word, according to what is attainable (ἐφικτός) for us, not opposing (ἐναντιόομαι) the clearer (τρανότερος) conception of the holy angels about him, but hastening (σπεύδω) daily (ὁσημέραι) toward that in clearness (τρανότης) and articulation (διάρθρωσις). As one not having read (ἀναγιγνώσκω) our sacred writings, Celsus answers (ἀποκρίνομαι) himself as from us that we say the angels coming down from God (παρὰ θεοῦ) for benefit (εὐεργεσία) of men are some other kind (γένος), and says that as is likely they would be called by us daemons; not seeing that the name (ὄνομα) of daemons is not even neutral (μέσον) like that of men, among whom some are good/refined (ἀστεῖοι) and some base (φαῦλοι), nor good (ἀστεῖον), of the sort that the name of gods is, being applied (τάσσω) not to base things, to demons (δαιμόνια) or to statues (ἀγάλματα) or to animals (ζῷα), but by those who have known (γιγνώσκω) the things of God to those truly more divine (θειότεροι) and blessed (μακάριοι). But always the name of daemons is applied to the base powers (δυνάμεις) outside the grosser (παχύτερος) body (σῶμα), leading astray (πλανάω) and distracting (περισπάω) men and dragging them down (καθέλκω) from God and the supercelestial things (ὑπερουράνια) to the affairs (πράγματα) here.

pass_b_english: For it is not reasonable to call upon angels without first acquiring a knowledge of them that is beyond human reach. And even supposing that this knowledge of them, wonderful and secret as it is, were attained, that very knowledge, by showing what their nature is and what task each of them is appointed to, will not allow anyone to venture to pray to any other than the God over all, who suffices for all things, through our Saviour, the Son of God. He is the “Word” (John 1:1), and Wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24), and Truth (John 14:6), and all else that the writings of God’s prophets and of Jesus’ apostles say of him.

For the holy angels of God to be gracious to us and to do everything on our behalf, it is enough that our disposition toward God should imitate, as far as human nature can, their purpose, as they imitate God; and that our understanding of his Son, the Word, so far as we can attain it, should not be at odds with the holy angels’ clearer understanding of him, but should press on toward it every day in clearness and precision.

Celsus, as one who has not read our sacred Scriptures, answers himself as if speaking for us, saying that we call the angels who come down from God for the benefit of men some other kind of being; and he says that presumably we would call them demons. He does not see that the name “demons” is not even neutral, as the name “men” is, among whom some are good and some bad. Nor is it a good name, as the name “gods” is, which is applied, not to base things, whether demons or statues or animals, but, by those who know the things of God, to beings that are truly more divine and blessed. The name “demons,” on the other hand, is always applied to the wicked powers that are outside the grosser body, which lead men astray and distract them and drag them down from God and from the things above the heavens to the affairs of this world.
notes: Only λόγος carries quotation marks in Koetschau’s text; σοφία and ἀλήθεια are titles of Christ drawn from Scripture, cited as clear allusions: John 1:1 (Word), 1 Corinthians 1:24 (Christ the wisdom of God; Proverbs 8 also possible), John 14:6 (the truth). ‘Call upon’ (καλέσαι) means invoke in prayer, as the next sentence shows. ἄλλο τι γένος παρὰ θεοῦ: read παρὰ θεοῦ with καταβαίνοντας (‘who come down from God’); a reading ‘some kind other than a god’ is grammatically possible and would fit Celsus’s question ‘gods or some other kind’. ‘Purpose’ renders προαίρεσις (deliberate choice, will). ‘Statues’ renders ἀγάλματα (cult images). ‘Outside the grosser body’ (ἔξω τοῦ παχυτέρου σώματος): powers not clothed in the coarse body humans have; Origen does not say they are wholly bodiless. ‘Things above the heavens’ = τὰ ὑπερουράνια. No direct Scripture quotation beyond the titles of Christ.

Open doubt (review): 5.5 ἄλλο τι γένος παρὰ θεοῦ: kept as 'angels who come down from God'; the reading 'some kind other than a god' is recorded in translator_notes. Low risk, so the verdict is still pass.
